title: How to Redesign Your Organization's Workflows for AI (and Tell If It Worked)
summary: Learn how to redesign workflows for AI across your organization in five steps, then use a six-signal scorecard to check whether the redesign worked.
body_markdown:
**Quick answer:** To redesign workflows for AI, pick a process that passes through several teams, such as employee onboarding (HR, then the hiring manager, then IT). Choose one with repeated, brainstorming, or writing tasks. Record each step's owner and wait time, and remove steps that serve no purpose. Assign each task to AI, to AI with a person, or to a person, based on your tools, information, and reviewers. Rebuild with fewer handoffs and one owner. Then compare six signals with your starting numbers: **AI use, handoffs and waits, review workload, contact between teams, rework, and business results** .


A common approach is to add AI to the way work already runs. A 2025[Faros AI study of more than 10,000 developers](https://www.faros.ai/blog/ai-software-engineering) found that teams using AI heavily merged 98% more pull requests (proposed code changes). The time those changes spent in review rose 91%. Faros says slow steps later in the process, such as review, were absorbing the gains.


The alternative is to redesign the work itself. Deloitte's 2026 research found that organizations that redesign work are[twice as likely to exceed the return on investment they expected from AI](https://www.deloitte.com/ca/en/services/consulting/perspectives/ai-work-redesign-value-creation.html) . It also describes a European telecom that gained about 5% in productivity by adding AI without redesign. It gained about 30% when roughly 90% of its rollout effort went into redesigning how people and AI share the work.


Below are five steps, then a six-signal scorecard to check the result. It is written for organization leaders, including engineering leaders and HR directors.


## What does it mean to redesign workflows for AI?


A workflow is the series of tasks that turns a request into a finished result, such as a new employee ready to start. People, software, and AI do the tasks, and the work passes from one to the next. Each pass is a handoff. To redesign a workflow for AI is to change which steps exist, who or what does each one, and where work waits.


### Workflow redesign, restructuring, and reorganizing: what each changes


Workflow redesign changes which steps the work goes through and who does them. Restructuring changes how the organization is set up: teams, management layers, and roles. Reorganizing moves people between teams or changes who reports to whom. Deloitte's guidance is to redesign the work before you redesign the workforce, and this guide follows that order. Headcount is a separate decision from all three.


## Why adding AI to an existing workflow often does not improve results


### Tasks get faster, but review does not


AI speeds up the person doing a task, not the person who has to review, approve, or accept the result. Faros also found that the average size of a pull request grew 154%, which makes each one slower to review. The same thing happens anywhere one team produces faster than another can handle it, such as HR opening onboarding requests faster than IT can work through them. Worklytics describes this in its piece on the[AI productivity paradox](https://www.worklytics.co/blog/the-ai-productivity-paradox-why-ai-is-speeding-up-work--but-slowing-down-companies) : the slow point moves to the review and approval steps.


### AI also speeds up outdated steps


Nick Colisto, CIO of Avery Dennison, argues in a CIO.com column that every workflow reflects past decisions. AI can run an outdated process faster without making it simpler. In his example, AI can route purchase approvals, but it cannot decide whether six approvals are still necessary.


## Step 1: Find the workflows worth redesigning


Start with work that passes through more than one team. Employee onboarding is one example: it goes from HR to the hiring manager to IT. Every handoff from one team to the next is a place for work to sit. In each workflow, list the tasks that suit AI. Step 3 decides which of them AI does alone.


- **Repeated tasks.** The same task happens often in the same way, such as answering the same policy questions from new hires or entering the same details into three systems.
- **Brainstorming.** Someone has to come up with options before the work can start, such as ideas for a new hire's first-week schedule. AI can list options, and a person chooses.
- **Writing and other creative work.** Someone has to produce wording from a blank page, such as a welcome email or a training outline. AI can write a first version, and a person edits it.


### Start with where AI is already used


Before you redesign, find out who already uses AI and for what, including tools people brought themselves. In the 2024 Work Trend Index, a Microsoft and LinkedIn survey of 31,000 knowledge workers, 78% of AI users said they bring their own AI tools to work. Check four places:


- Admin reports in each AI tool.
- License and spend records, including expense claims for AI subscriptions.
- Company sign-in records that show which AI apps people log in to.
- A short anonymous survey asking which AI tools people use and for what.


Admin reports show one tool at a time. A people analytics platform such as Worklytics combines usage data from tools like Microsoft Copilot, ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and Cursor in one[AI adoption dashboard](https://www.worklytics.co/measureai) . Usage data means how often each person or team uses each tool, and you can split it by team, role, department, and manager. If you find little use, redesigning around AI may be premature. Help people adopt it first.


Worklytics sample report (fictional data): days per week each department uses AI, from none (red) to four or more (dark green).


## Step 2: Map how work moves, then cut the steps it does not need


### Break the workflow into steps


For each workflow you picked, write down every step, who is responsible, what goes in, what comes out, and who receives it next. Record two times for each step: how long the item waits before anyone starts, and how long the work itself takes. AI usually shortens the work time, but waits often stay the same unless you change the steps. Ask the people who do the work, not only their managers. Here is an example for employee onboarding:


Step Owner Input Output Waits for Passed to


1. Create employee record HR operations Signed offer Employee record Background check Hiring manager


2. Approve system access Hiring manager Access request Approval Manager's inbox IT


3. Set up laptop and accounts IT Approval Working laptop and logins Equipment delivery New hire


Keep these numbers as your starting numbers, also called a baseline, and compare against them after the change. Use the median wait (the middle value) rather than the average, because a few very long waits distort an average.


### Find where the work waits


Work waits at handoffs and approvals. Ticketing, finance, and workflow software record when an item entered and left each stage. Engineering's code review tools show how long changes wait for review and how many are waiting.


Worklytics's[organizational network analysis](https://www.worklytics.co/ona-data-analytics-software-worklytics) adds the people side. It uses data about who contacts whom, how often, and when, from email, calendar, chat, and meeting tools, not what is said. It shows which teams work together, which have little contact, and which people link two teams. It shows contact, not waiting time, so pair it with the timestamps above. Meeting data can also hint at approval levels, such as how often a team's meetings include several levels of management.


Worklytics sample report (fictional data): contact between six offices. Dark blue is heavy contact, orange is very little.


Worklytics sample report (fictional data): each bubble is a department. Higher means more meetings with over 3 levels of leadership, further right more meetings with over 8 attendees.


### Remove steps that exist because a human was slow


Colisto's four moves, in order, are simplify, standardize, redesign, then automate. Do the first two before you decide what AI does. Simplify by removing approvals, reports, and handoffs that no longer serve a purpose. Standardize by agreeing on one way of doing each remaining step. His test for the first move: if we were designing this process today, would we build it the same way? Keep approvals that guard against costly mistakes, such as access to sensitive systems.


## Step 3: Decide which tasks AI does, which AI helps with, and which stay with people


Deloitte's guidance is to break your most important workflows into tasks and decide which to automate, augment, or elevate. In plain terms, each task goes to one of three places: AI does it alone, AI helps a person do it, or a person does it. These four questions sort each task:


Ask about each task If yes Example


Does it happen often and follow clear rules? AI does it, and a person spot-checks the results. Answering common policy questions


Does it need ideas, options, or a first draft that a person then improves? AI helps, and a person decides. Drafting a first-week plan for a new hire


Would a mistake be costly (legal, safety, or money)? A person decides. AI prepares the material. Approving access to sensitive systems


Does it depend on a relationship or on context only a person has? A person does it. Welcoming a new hire and setting expectations


Worklytics sorts AI activity into task types such as writing code, research, analysis, summaries, and email, using[usage data and activity signals, not the text of prompts](https://www.worklytics.co/blog/how-to-identify-which-tasks-your-employees-are-automating-with-ai) . Treat the result as a starting point and check it with the teams who do the work.


Worklytics sample report (fictional data): what people use each AI tool for.


### Then check what you have before you assign each task


The four questions show which tasks suit AI. What you have decides how many you can hand over now. Check these four resources for each task AI would do or help with:


Resource Ask If the answer is no


AI tool and budget Does the team have an AI tool for this task, and does the budget cover more licenses if it spreads? Keep the task with people, or approve a tool first.


Information Can the tool read what the task needs, such as policy documents or the employee record? Keep the task with a person until the information is in one place the tool can use.


Reviewer time Does a named person have time each week to check the AI's work? Give AI fewer tasks. Work that nobody has time to review sits waiting.


Skills Does anyone know how to give the AI clear instructions and spot a wrong answer? Train a small group first and start with one task.


For example, answering common policy questions suits AI. If the policies sit in scattered files the tool cannot read, a person keeps answering until they are in one place. The tools you found in Step 1 show what you have today. As you add tools, information, and reviewers, move more tasks to AI.


## Step 4: Rebuild the workflow around the tasks you assigned


### Cut handoffs and name owners


Fewer, clearer handoffs are better than many small ones. Write down where a person must approve and what sends a case to a senior person (an escalation). Then move each approval to the person closest to the work who has enough information to decide. Name one owner for the redesigned workflow and one for each AI step. The AI step owner looks after the tool, the instructions given to the AI (prompts), and the quality checks. Decide in advance what happens when AI output is wrong or a case does not fit the rules.


### Give code reviewers enough time (engineering)


If your engineers will submit far more pull requests, reviewing them needs real people and time. Try smaller pull requests and a rotating schedule so reviewers share the load. Add an AI first pass followed by a human sign-off, and name one person responsible for how long changes wait for review. Worklytics[connects to engineering tools](https://www.worklytics.co/engineering-effectiveness) such as GitHub and Jira. Check how long changes wait for review every week for the first three months.


Illustrative engineering dashboard with example numbers, including pull request reviews and outstanding pull requests.


### Pilot one workflow, then check how teams are organized


Redesign one workflow first, and pick one that runs often enough to compare before and after within a few weeks. Compare its results with your starting numbers before you apply the same changes elsewhere. Once it works, check whether your teams are still organized the right way, because roles change when AI takes over tasks. You may need to restructure or reorganize if managers now have too many or too few direct reports. A 2024 Worklytics analysis found that[managers with more than 7 direct reports were more likely to work 10 to 13 hour workdays](https://www.worklytics.co/blog/using-ona-to-find-optimal-team-size) . With too few, teams often suffer from over-management: the manager gets too involved in the details. The post suggests 4 to 7 as the best range, depending on the role and type of work. It names no sample size, so test the range against your own numbers.


## Step 5: Bring the people doing the work into the redesign


People are less likely to adopt a redesign they do not understand. Bain surveyed 976 executives, managers, and employees whose roles were affected by a new organizational structure (fielded in late 2025). It found that[AI-related changes underperformed other kinds of organizational change](https://www.bain.com/insights/ai-focused-organizational-changes-underperform-other-reorganizations-snap-chart/) . Fewer than 40% said the scope and reason for the AI change were clear. Targeted support and coaching reached 59% of AI transformations, against 70% of change efforts in general.


Involve the people who do the work in the mapping and the redesign. Give them a one-page explanation of what is changing, why now, what stays the same, and what it means for their role. Then say when you will share the results.


## How to tell if the redesign worked


Compare the results with the baseline you saved in Step 2, and track outcomes, not AI activity. Colisto makes the same point: measure cycle time (how long work takes from start to finish), quality, customer satisfaction, and cost, not the number of prompts submitted.


### The six signals, and what to do when one gets worse


Signal What to track, and where it comes from Warning sign What to do


1. AI use in the workflow How many people use AI each week and how often, by team, role, and manager (AI tool reports, or a platform such as Worklytics). Only a few people use it, or managers use it far less than their teams. Check whether managers use AI themselves, then whether old approval steps remain.


2. Handoffs and waits Number of handoffs and approvals, and the median wait at each (ticketing or workflow software). The same number of handoffs, or longer waits than before. AI was added on top of the old process. Remove a handoff, or let someone closer to the work approve.


3. Review workload Items per reviewer, items waiting for review, and reviewers' hours in meetings (engineering and calendar tools). The number of items waiting grows faster than reviewers can clear them. Add reviewers, send smaller batches, or let low-risk items pass automatic checks instead of a person.


4. Contact between teams How often teams that work together are in contact, and any one person the work depends on (collaboration data, such as Worklytics). Two teams that used to work together barely talk, or one person is the only link between them. Restore contact with a shared channel or regular meeting, or name one person to link them.


5. Rework and quality Items sent back for rework, defects, escalations, and complaints (quality systems). Work gets faster but rework or complaints go up too. Slow the rollout and put a human check back before customers see the work.


6. Business results Time from start to finish, cost, and customer satisfaction (business systems). Steps get faster but time, cost, or satisfaction do not improve. Find the step where work now waits longest and redesign that step.


Do not read signal 1 alone. If many people use AI but the handoffs and waits are the same as before, the old steps are still in place. Worklytics describes a[four-layer efficiency map](https://www.worklytics.co/blog/is-ai-actually-saving-time-in-your-company) : who uses AI, how deeply, what productivity changes, and what the recovered time is worth.


### When to check


Check at 30 days, 90 days, and six months. Early checks cover behavior: AI use, handoffs, and items waiting for review. Later checks cover results: rework, time from start to finish, and satisfaction. A redesign disrupts work at first, so do not judge it on the first month. If a similar team or workflow did not change, compare against it, so a busy season does not look like a result.


## Where work usually waits, by function


These are common waiting points. Check them first.


Function Where work usually waits What to measure


Engineering Code review and release approval Review time, number of changes waiting, size of each change


HR Onboarding requests and policy questions Time to first response, handoffs between HR and IT


Finance Approvals that must happen one after another, and matching records (reconciliation) Days in approval, invoices sent back for rework


Customer support Cases passed from one support level to the next Time to resolution, share of cases passed up


Sales Quotes waiting on discount approval Days waiting for approval, number of approvers


## What data can and cannot tell you


Usage and collaboration data show who uses AI and who works with whom, not whether the work was good. No single tool covers everything. Ticketing and workflow software holds approval times. Engineering platforms such as DX, LinearB, and Faros cover developer productivity and delivery. Microsoft Viva Insights covers Microsoft 365 collaboration data. People analytics platforms such as Worklytics combine AI usage and collaboration data from many connected tools. Whichever you pick, know the limits:


- It sees who used what and when, not what was written. Worklytics uses usage data only, never the content of prompts or outputs, so it cannot judge a decision or a line of code.
- It only sees connected tools. Work in unconnected systems, in person, or on paper is missing.
- It shows who is in contact, not how long work waited. Approval waits come from your workflow software.
- Some numbers are estimates, and patterns are not causes. Time-saved figures come from models, and task types are inferred from usage signals, so check both with the teams who do the work. If two things move together, ask the team why before you act.
- It needs agreed privacy rules. Report results for groups, not individuals, tell people what is measured, and agree the rules with legal and employee representatives first. Worklytics removes names or replaces them with codes (anonymizes or pseudonymizes) and reports at team level.


Worklytics' own diagram of its privacy proxy. Email addresses from tools such as Outlook, Gmail, and Google Drive are replaced with coded identifiers before analysis.


## Frequently asked questions


### How do you redesign a workflow for AI?


Pick a workflow that passes through several teams, such as employee onboarding. Write down each step's owner and wait, remove steps that serve no purpose, and assign each task to AI, to AI with a person, or to a person. Rebuild with fewer handoffs and one named owner, then compare with your starting numbers.


### What is the difference between workflow redesign and automation?


Automation applies technology to the steps you already have. Redesign changes the steps first: it removes, merges, or reorders them before you decide what to automate. CIO's Nick Colisto puts it as redesign first, automate second.


### How is AI changing workflows?


AI does or helps with individual tasks, so the slow part shifts to the steps where work is handed on, reviewed, and approved. In a 2025 Faros AI study, teams using AI heavily merged 98% more pull requests (proposed code changes), and review time rose 91%.


### Should you restructure or reorganize teams before redesigning workflows?


Redesign the workflow first, as Deloitte advises. Once it works, check roles and how many people report to each manager, and treat headcount as a separate decision.


### What data do you need to redesign workflows for AI?


Four kinds help: AI use by team and role, who works with whom, when work enters and leaves each step, and quality and business results. A platform such as Worklytics can supply the first two, but not approval waits or quality.


If you want to see which teams use AI and which teams work together before you redesign anything, you can[book a demo](https://www.worklytics.co/get-started) . Worklytics shows this from your own data at team level, without reading message content. If you already have these numbers from other tools, the six signals work just as well.
